• Fear of Communism spreading to Eastern Europe during the Cold War
• Showed the global impact of the Russian Revolution

Key Figures:
• Vladimir Lenin: Bolshevik leader
• Leon Trotsky: Initially Menshevik, joined Lenin in 1917

The Great Depression:
• Massive global economic recession
• Led to: bank failures, high unemployment, inflation
• Dramatic drops in GDP, industrial production, and stock market prices

Causes:
• Collapse of international trade due to restrictive trade practices

Effects:
• Hit non-industrial countries more harshly
• Prices of raw materials and food fell more sharply than manufactured goods

Political Effects:
• Helped militarists take power in Japan
• Major factor in Hitler's rise to power in Germany (January 1933)

The New Deal (1933-1938):
• Program by President F.D. Roosevelt
• Sought to stimulate the economy and redistribute wealth

Origin: 'Fascies' (rods and axes symbolizing authority in ancient Rome)

Features:
• Extreme, aggressive nationalism
• Glorification of strength and military virtues
• Survival of the fittest among nations
• Supreme importance of a national leader (unconditional authority)
• State control of all means of communication
• Tendency towards racism (belief in Aryan superiority)

Appeal of Fascism:
• Attracted petty-bourgeois groups (shopkeepers, entrepreneurs)
• Attracted unemployed people
• Attracted youth and ex-soldiers
• Attracted intellectuals dissatisfied with post-war situation
• Attracted gangsters

slide_title: Rise of Fascism in Italy and Nazism in Germany
basic_presentation:
Italian Fascism:
• Led by Benito Mussolini
• 1919: Organized the Fascist Party
• October 1922: March on Rome
• King Victor Emmanuel III appointed Mussolini as Prime Minister

German Nazism:
• Led by Adolf Hitler
• National Socialist Party (Nazi Party)
• 1923: Attempted to overthrow Weimar Republic (Hitler imprisoned)
• In prison, wrote 'Mein Kampf' (My Struggle)
• January 1933: Hitler became Chancellor

Reasons for Nazi Success:
• German national pride severely harmed by WWI
• Versailles Treaty unpopular
• Economic distress and inflation
• Political discontent against the Weimar Republic

slide_title: Franco's Spain and Japan in the 1930s
basic_presentation:
Franco's Spain:
• General Francisco Franco established right-wing authoritarian regime after Spanish Civil War (1936-1939)
• Received support from Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy
• Was NOT a fascist (had no Fascist ideology, no mass popular movement)

Japan's Regime (1933-1945):
• Sometimes described as 'Fascist'
• Similarities with European Fascism:
   - Authoritarianism
   - Racism (belief in 'master race')
   - Militarism
   - Aggressive nationalism
   - Hatred of Marxism
• Differences:
   - Appeared in a different social and political context
   - Was NOT Fascist in the European sense

slide_title: World War II: Alliance Systems and Appeasement
basic_presentation:
Axis Powers:
• Rome-Berlin Axis (1936): Germany and Italy
• Tripartite Pact (September 27, 1940): Germany, Italy, Japan (Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis)

Allied Powers:
• Initially: Britain, France, Poland
• Later: USSR, USA, China

Appeasement Policy:
• Britain and France made concessions to Hitler to avoid war
• Reasons: Not ready for war, economic crisis (Depression), US isolationism

Key Events Before the War:
• 1931: Japan took Manchuria
• 1933: Hitler withdrew Germany from League of Nations
• 1936: Hitler militarized the Rhineland
• 1938: Hitler annexed Austria and Sudetenland (Munich Agreement)
• 1939: Italy occupied Albania

slide_title: World War II: Course of the War (1939-1941)
basic_presentation:
Outbreak: September 1, 1939 - Hitler invaded Poland
• Britain and France declared war on Germany (September 3, 1939)

Blitzkrieg (Lightning War):
• Coordinated attacks of air force and fast-moving ground forces
• Germany quickly conquered most of Europe

The Phony War (May 1940):
• No real fighting on the Western Front
• Ended when Germany invaded Denmark, Norway (April 1940)

Fall of France (June 1940):
• Germany invaded Netherlands, Belgium, France (May 10, 1940)
• June 14: Paris surrendered
• Italy declared war on Britain and France (June 10, 1940)
• Vichy France puppet government set up

Battle of Britain (1940):
• Hitler launched attacks from the air
• British used 'Radar' to locate attackers
• Churchill refused to seek peace

slide_title: World War II: Course of the War (1941-1945)
basic_presentation:
Operation Barbarossa (June 22, 1941):
• Germany invaded the Soviet Union
• 'Great Patriotic War' began
• German blitzkrieg failed to bring desired results
• Soviet counterattacks defeated Germans near Moscow

Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941):
• Japanese surprise attack on US naval base in Hawaii
• US declared war on Japan (December 8, 1941)
• Germany and Italy declared war on US (December 11, 1941)
• Made the war fully a world war

North Africa Campaign:
• 1942: German forces nearly took Egypt
• Late October 1942: British launched major attack
• May 1943: Axis forces in North Africa surrendered

slide_title: World War II: Turning Points and End
basic_presentation:
Invasion of Italy (July 1943):
• King Victor Emmanuel III deposed Mussolini
• Mussolini rescued by German forces
• June 4, 1944: Allied troops occupied Rome
• Mussolini later captured and executed by Italian communists

D-Day (June 6, 1944):
• Operation Overlord - US, British, Canadian forces landed at Normandy
• Major breakthrough in Allied reconquest of Europe

Soviet Advances:
• Operation Bagration (June 22, 1944): Massive Soviet offensive
• By early 1944, Red Army reached border of Poland

End of War in Europe:
• April 30, 1945: Hitler committed suicide
• V-E Day (May 8, 1945) - Germany surrendered

slide_title: World War II: The Pacific Theater and Atomic Bombs
basic_presentation:
Pacific Theater:
• Battle of Midway Island (1942): Decisive defeat for Japanese navy
• By 1944, US forces were getting ready to invade mainland Japan

Yalta Conference (February 1945):
• Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalin met to discuss post-war Europe
• Germany to be divided into American, British, French, and Soviet zones
• Planned for UN establishment

Potsdam Conference (July 1945):
• Agreed on peace settlement with Germany
• Drew up plans for Japan's surrender

Atomic Bombs:
• August 6, 1945: Hiroshima (80,000 killed instantly)
• August 9, 1945: Nagasaki (40,000 killed instantly)
• Death toll rose to about 200,000 from radiation sickness

August 15, 1945: Japan surrendered (V-J Day)

slide_title: Restoration of Imperial Rule and British Ascendancy
basic_presentation:
May 1941: Emperor Haile Selassie restored to the throne with British help.

British Ascendancy:
• Britain effectively became the occupying power replacing Italy
• Considerable tension between Ethiopia and Britain
• Ethiopia expected full sovereignty; Britain considered independence a long-term objective

Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement of 1942:
• Confirmed Ethiopia's status as a sovereign state
• But almost every article underlined Ethiopia's dependency on Britain:
   - British minister had primacy over all other diplomatic representatives
   - British military mission to train the new Ethiopian army
   - British citizens occupied key posts (civil and military advisers, police force, financial system)
   - Ogaden and strategic areas under British administration

slide_title: The Second Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement and Territorial Issues
basic_presentation:
Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement of 1944:
• Restored some sovereign rights
• British minister's precedence was lifted
• Ethiopian army no longer controlled by British officials
• British agreed to restore parts of the Ethio-Djibouti railway

British Plans for Partition:
• Planned to separate Eritrea and the Ogaden from Ethiopia
• Proposed uniting parts of Tigray with Eritrean highlands (separate Tigrean state)
• Proposed incorporating Ogaden into Greater Somalia
• Envisaged partition of Eritrea, with western lowlands to Sudan

Ethiopia's Response:
• Became a founding member of the UN (1945)
• Made strong demands for both the Ogaden and Eritrea
• British withdrew from parts of Ogaden (1948), restored entire region (1954)

Eritrea Under British Administration (1941-1951):

Local Groups in Eritrea:
• Unionist Party: Demanded union with Ethiopia (largest political group)
• Muslim League, Liberal Progressive Party, Pro-Italian Group: Demanded independence

Resolution Process:
• Four Powers Commission (Britain, France, Soviet Union, USA) - could not resolve
• Referred to UN in 1948
• UN Commission (Burma, Guatemala, Norway, Pakistan, South Africa) - divided

UN General Assembly Decision (December 2, 1950):
• Voted for federation with Ethiopia
• Federation came into effect in 1952
• Eritrea became federated with Ethiopia

Following British departure, the US became Ethiopia's main ally.

Kagnew Communications Station Agreement (May 22, 1953):
• US given 25-year lease on the Kagnew station in Asmara
• One of the largest radio relay and communications monitoring stations in the world
• Used to monitor Soviet radio communications
• Named after the first Ethiopian Battalion that fought in the Korean War

US Aid:
• $5 million to equip and train Ethiopian armed forces
• By the 1970s, Ethiopia absorbed 60% of total US military aid to Africa
• Ethiopian armed forces became totally dependent on the US for military hardware

Other US Contributions:
• Ethiopian Air Lines (1945)
• Imperial Highway Authority (1951)
• Education system modeled after the American system
• Peace Corps Program (1960s)

Agriculture:
• Over 60% of GDP and 80% of labor force
• Coffee and agricultural commodities comprised over 90% of exports
• Underdeveloped due to drought, poor infrastructure, government neglect

Land Tenure System (Pre-1974):

Northern Provinces:
• Rist: Communal land ownership based on kinship
• Most peasants held at least some rist land

Southern Provinces:
• Gult: Right to collect tribute from peasants (granted by the state)
• Gabbar System: Peasants reduced to tenants, paying rent and forced labor

Other Forms:
• Samon: Land granted to the Ethiopian Orthodox Church
• Mengist: Government property
• Maderia: Land granted to officials, war veterans, and patriots

slide_title: Land Reform Issues and Agricultural Development
basic_presentation:
Negative Impacts of Feudal Land Tenure:
• Peasants had no security of tenure
• Landowners could evict peasants anytime
• Acceleration of privatization in the south

Land Tax Decrees (1942 onwards):
• Fixed tax based on land classification (lam, lam-taf, taf)
• Used gasha (40 hectares) as measurement
• Faced stiff resistance from landowners

Agricultural Development (Imperial Period):
• Less than 2% of budget allocated to agriculture
• Agricultural production grew below population growth rate
• Commercial agriculture expanded (Tendaho Cotton Plantations, Setiti Humara)
• Minimum Package Program (MPP) introduced (1971)
• Chilalo Agricultural Development Unit (CADU)

Demand for Land Reform:
• Students led 'Land to the Tiller' movement (1965 onwards)
• Land Reform and Development Authority (1965)
• Parliament resisted reforms (landlords represented)
• 1972-74 drought and famine: hundreds of thousands died

Trade:
• Constituted only 7% of GDP in the 1960s
• Coffee was the leading cash crop (50-65% of exports)
• Other exports: hides, skins, pulses, oilseeds
• Major imports: textiles, machinery, chemicals
• Major trading partners: USA (70% of coffee), Italy, Japan
• Balance of trade registered annual deficits (1953-1974)

Industry:
• Less than 5% of GDP in 1975
• Employed only about 60,000 people

Domestic Trade:
• Addis Ababa remained commercial centre (Mercato replaced Arada/Piazza)
• Role of Greek, Armenian, Arab traders challenged by emerging national traders

Development Plans:
• National Economic Council (1954/55)
• First and second five-year plans (1950s-1960s)
• Failed to achieve meaningful results

Nature of the State:
• Absolutist state, reaching its height of power
• Top-heavy, secularized bureaucracy
• Imperial myth centered on the Emperor
• Words of the Emperor were final on appointments and decisions

Institutions of Control:
• Military: Army, Imperial Bodyguard, Police Force
• Department of Public Security: Elaborate intelligence network
• Highest budget allocations to Ministry of Defence and Department of Public Security

Administrative Structure:
• 14 provinces (teklay-gizats), each under a governor general
• Sub-divided into awrajas (sub-provinces), weredas (districts), mikitil-weredas (sub-districts)
• High-ranking landed nobles held all important offices

Education System:
• Designed to produce manpower for the bureaucracy
• Haile Selassie I Secondary School (1943), General Wingate School (1946)
• University College of Addis Ababa (1950)
• Haile Selassie I University (1961)

Promulgated on the silver jubilee of the Emperor's coronation.

Reasons for Revision:
• Incorporation of Eritrea (more advanced constitution)

Key Provisions:
• Universal adult suffrage
• Elected Chamber of Deputies (nominal)
• Bicameral parliament (Senate and Chamber of Deputies)
• Senate appointive; Chamber nominally elected
• Low popular participation

Consolidation of Absolutism:
• 'The person of the Emperor is sacred, his dignity is inviolable, and his power is indisputable'
• Human rights provisions accompanied by 'in accordance with the law' or 'within the limits of the law'

Cult of Personality:
• Major landmarks named after the Emperor
• Birth and coronation days celebrated as national holidays

slide_title: Plots and Conspiracies Against the Emperor
basic_presentation:
Immediate Post-Liberation Groups:
• Returnees (exiles with the Emperor)
• Collaborators (worked with Italians)
• Patriots (played major role in liberation struggle)

Dajjach Belay Zeleke:
• Prominent patriot leader in Gojjam
• Opposed the Emperor as a deserter
• Rejected appointment to southern province
• Surrendered in 1943 after negotiations, but was betrayed
• Broke out of jail, caught, and executed by hanging

Bitwodded Negash Bezabih:
• Famous patriot leader, grandson of Negus Tekle-Haimanot
• Led conspiracy to assassinate Haile Selassie (1951)
• Betrayed by Dajjach Geressu Duki
• Arrested and sentenced to imprisonment

Blatta Takele Wolde-Hawaryat:
• Shewa patriot leader, longest opposition
• Opposed Emperor's return from exile
• Made several attempts to overthrow him
• Killed in shoot-out with police (November 1969)

Leaders: The 'Neway Brothers'
• Brigadier General Mengistu Neway (Commander of the Imperial Bodyguard)
• Germame Neway (the mind/spirit behind the coup)

Supporters:
• Radical intellectuals
• Colonel Worqneh Gebeyehu (Commander of Security Forces)
• Brigadier General Tsege Dibu (Police Force Commander)

Course of Events:
• December 13, 1960: Plotters took hostages at Genete Leul Palace
• Crown Prince Asfawosen appointed as constitutional monarch
• 'People's Government' announced with progressive aristocracy

Demands:
• Improve economic, social, and political problems

Reasons for Failure:
• No attempt to win support of army and air force
• University students supported, but army and air force remained loyal
• Church condemned the coup makers

Outcome:
• Coup suppressed by December 17
• Neway brothers massacred hostages and fled
• Germame committed suicide; Mengistu captured and executed

Common Causes:
• Increasing state pressure on peasant resources
• Ethno-nationalist sentiments
• Land and tax issues
• Maladministration

Woyane Rebellion (Tigray, 1943):
• Led by Blatta Hayle Mariam Redda
• Initial victories, captured Mekelle
• Crushed by imperial forces with British air support

Bale Peasant Rebellion (1963-1970):
• Started in El Kere district
• Local discontent over land and tax issues, opposition to Christian settlement
• Leaders: Kahin Abdi (Somali), Waqo Gutu (Oromo)
• Crushed by massive military operation (1967-1970)

Gojjam Peasant Rebellion (1968):
• Causes: New agricultural income tax, arrogance of governor Tsehayu
• Strong in Motta and Kolla Dega Damot districts
• Government concessions (new tax abandoned, unpopular officials removed)
• Rebellion suppressed by military campaign

slide_title: Armed Struggle in Eritrea and Other Movements
basic_presentation:
Eritrean Armed Struggle:
• Federation came into effect (1952), but imperial government wanted direct rule
• 1962: Eritrea became the 14th province of Ethiopia

Separatist Movements:
• Eritrean Liberation Movement (ELM, 1958) - discovered and disbanded
• Eritrean Liberation Front (ELF, 1960) - launched armed struggle (1961)
   - Supported by radical Arab states (Egypt, Syria, Iraq)
   - Dominated by Muslims, later split into three groups
• Eritrean People's Liberation Forces (EPLF, 1972) - formed from splinter groups

Mecha-Tulama Self-Help Association (1963):
• Promoted Oromo self-identity
• Provided education, water supply, communication, health facilities
• Became politically active, considered a threat
• Brigadier General Taddesse Birru (elected president) arrested (1966)
• Banned (1966), led to rise of more militant Oromo nationalism

Causes: Expansion of secondary and higher education

Phases of the Movement:

Phase 1 (1950s):
• Demanded improvement in learning facilities and services
• Student councils as organizations

Phase 2 (After 1960):
• More radical demands
• Influenced by the 1960 coup, Eritrean resistance

Phase 3 (Mid-1960s onwards):
• Revolutionary phase
• Birth of 'crocodiles' (radical core, Marxist ideas)
• February 1965: Demonstration against feudal land tenure ('Land to the Tiller!')
• 1969: Raised issue of rights of nations and nationalities

Student Organizations:
• University Students' Union of Addis Ababa (USUAA) - Tagel
• Ethiopian Students' Union in North America (ESUNA) - Challenge
• Ethiopian Students' Union in Europe (ESUE) - Tataq

Confrontation: December 28, 1969 - Tilahun Gizaw killed, violence escalated

slide_title: The 1974 Revolution: Causes and Popular Upsurge
basic_presentation:
Causes of the Revolution:
• Failure to effect significant economic and political reforms
• Rising inflation and corruption
• Famine affecting several provinces (especially Wollo)

The Popular Upsurge (January-June 1974):

January 1974: Negele-Borena Mutiny
• Fourth Brigade mutinied over provisions (food, water)
• Took commanding officers hostage
• Concessions made to mutineers encouraged spread of discontent

February 18, 1974: Revolution reached Addis Ababa
• Teachers went on strike (opposed Sector Review, demanded higher pay)
• University students joined demonstrations
• Taxi drivers struck against fuel price increases

Military Mutiny Spreads:
• Second Division (Asmara), Fourth Division (Addis Ababa), Air Force (Dabra Zayt) mutinied
• Soldiers demanded salary increases and political reforms
• Formed Coordinating Committee of the Armed Forces (precursor of the Derg)

Government Responses:
• February 1974: Akllu Habte Wold and cabinet forced to resign
• March 1974: Endalkachew Mekonnen appointed Prime Minister
• Promised reforms (constitutional reform)
• Allowed army significant salary increase

March 1974: General Strike
• Confederation of Ethiopian Labor Unions (CELU) staged successful general strike
• Paralyzed the entire nation, especially the capital

April 20, 1974: Muslim Demonstrations
• Estimated 100,000 Muslims and Christian sympathizers
• Demanded religious equality

April-May 1974: Coordinating Committee Actions
• Colonel Alem Zewd Tessema (chairman) arrested former officials
• But failed to contain unrest
• Endalkachew replaced committee with High National Security Commission

June 28, 1974: The Derg Formed
• 120 members from every military and police unit
• Major Mengistu Haile Mariam as chairman
• Major Atnafu Abate as vice-chairman

slide_title: The Derg Takes Control and Deposes the Emperor
basic_presentation:
The 'Creeping Coup' (June 28 - September 12, 1974):
• Derg professed loyalty to the Emperor
• Began arresting members of the aristocracy and high-ranking officials
• Forced out Prime Minister Endalkachew, replaced by Lij Mikael Imru

Derg's Motto: 'Ethiopia Tikdem' (Ethiopia First)

Deposition of the Emperor (September 12, 1974):
• Proclamation officially deposed Haile Selassie
• Suspended the Revised Constitution of 1955
• Dissolved Parliament
• Established Provisional Military Administrative Council (PMAC)
• General Aman Andom appointed Head of State

General Aman Andom's Challenges:
• Disagreed with Derg on three issues:
   - Size of the Derg (too large)
   - Eritrean insurgency (urged reconciliation)
   - Fate of political prisoners (opposed death penalty)

slide_title: Bloody Saturday and Consolidation of Power
basic_presentation:
October 7, 1974: Derg crushed civilian dissidents

November 23, 1974: Bloody Saturday
• General Aman Andom killed while resisting arrest
• 52 senior officials of the old regime executed
• About half a dozen leaders of military units opposing Derg executed
• Total of 60 victims (known as the 'sixty')

Significance of Bloody Saturday:
• Most damaging political blunder of the Derg
• Discredited the regime both at home and abroad
• Eliminated all moderate opposition

After Bloody Saturday:
• Brigadier General Tafari Banti became Chairman of PMAC and Head of State (November 28, 1974)
• Major Mengistu retained power as First Vice-Chairman
• Mengistu emerged as the decisive force in the Derg

slide_title: Early Reforms: Zemecha and Land Reform
basic_presentation:
Development through Cooperation Campaign (Zemecha):
• Announced October 1974, launched December 1974
• Aimed to mobilize university and secondary students to the countryside
• Explain socialist revolution and land reform to peasants
• Improve literacy rate
• Terminated June 1976 (EPRP members infiltrated and incited opposition)

Other Zemecha Campaigns:
• Yearnguadew Zemecha (Green Campaign, 1978) - rapid economic development
• Yemesrettimhirt Zemecha (Literacy Campaign, 1979) - some success
• Yeqeyi Kokeb Zemecha (Red Star Campaign, 1982) - solve Eritrean problem

Proclamation of Ethiopian Socialism:
• Changed slogan from 'Ethiopia Tikdem' to 'Ethiopian Socialism'
• March 1975: All royal titles revoked, proposed constitutional monarchy abandoned

Nationalization of Rural Land (March 1975):
• Abolished all private land ownership
• Set ceiling on family holdings at ten hectares
• Provided for formation of peasant associations (village, district, provincial levels)
• Peasant associations in charge of implementation in cooperation with Zemecha

Nationalization of Urban Land and Extra Houses (1975):
• All urban land and rentable dwellings nationalized
• Kebeles established as basic unit of urban government
• Served as instruments of socio-political control

Impact:
• Dismantled socio-economic basis of feudo-capitalism
• Replaced by a socialist socio-economic order
• Both rural and urban communities organized into hierarchy of associations

Marxist-Leninist Organizations Emerge:
• Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Party (EPRP / Ehapa)
• All-Ethiopian Socialist Movement (Meison)
• Workers' League (Wezlig)
• Ethiopian Marxist-Leninist Organization (Malerid)
• Ethiopian Oppressed Masses Revolutionary Struggle (Echa'at)
• Abyotaw Seded (Revolutionary Flame - launched by Mengistu)

Union of Marxist-Leninist Organizations (Emaledih - early 1977):
• Task: Identify strategies for creating a vanguard party
• Meison left the union (leaders killed or arrested)
• Other members (Echa'at, Wezlig, Malerid) expelled

Commission for Organizing the Party of the Workers of Ethiopia (COPEW - December 1979):
• Mengistu as chairman
• Workers' Party of Ethiopia (WPE) proclaimed (September 12, 1984)
• Mengistu became first secretary-general

Mass Organizations Created:
• All-Ethiopia Trade Union (AETU) - replaced CELU (1977)
• All-Ethiopia Peasants' Association (AEPA) / Ethiopian Peasants' Association (EPA)
• Revolutionary Ethiopian Women's Association (REWA - 1980)
• Revolutionary Ethiopian Youth Association (REYA - 1980)

People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia (PDRE - September 1987):
• Institute for the Study of Nationalities established
• Constitution drafted and ratified by 'referendum' (February 1987)
• National Shengo (supreme body) elected
• Mengistu became the country's first civilian president
• Still remained WPE's general secretary

Nature of the Regime:
• Members of the now-defunct Derg still ran the government
• Same people with different titles

1984/85 Famine:
• More severe than 1973/74 famine
• Affected nearly eight million people, killed about one million
• Clear manifestation of failure of regime's economic policy

Resettlement Policy:
• Permanent relocation of about 1.5 million people from north to south/southwest
• Rationale: Combat drought, avert famine, increase agricultural productivity
• Critics: Poorly planned, haphazardly executed, forceful relocation
• Thousands died from malaria and sleeping sickness
• 100,000 people died under the program
• Suspicions: Primary motive was to depopulate northern insurgency areas

Villagization Program (January 1985):
• Relocation of peasants into larger villages (40-300 families)
• Rationale: Better access to services, efficient resource use, hasten collectivization
• Critics: Impoverished peasants, reduced productive capacity, population control
• Services not delivered as promised

Major Challenges Facing the PMAC (1976-1977):
• Power struggle within the Derg
• EPRP attacked the Derg, demanding power transfer to civilian government
• Eritrean insurgents (ELF, EPLF) - encircled Asmara
• Ethiopian Democratic Union (EDU) - advancing from Sudan
• Somalia invaded Ethiopia (Ogaden War, 1977)

Power Struggle within the Derg:
• Summer 1976: Mengistu eliminated powerful members (Sisay Habte, Getachew Nadew, others)
• February 3, 1977: Palace coup - Colonel Daniel Asfaw arrested General Tafari Benti and others
• All key members of the PMAC were taken away and executed
• Mengistu declared himself the Derg's chairman
• November 1977: Atnafu Abaate eliminated - Mengistu in undisputed command

slide_title: The White Terror and Red Terror
basic_presentation:
White Terror (EPRP):
• Urban guerrilla warfare by EPRP against the Derg
• Assassinations of Derg supporters
• Attempt on Colonel Mengistu's life (September 23, 1976)

Red Terror (Derg):
• Government security forces systematically hunted down suspected EPRP members
• Between 1977 and 1978: Estimated 100,000 people killed or disappeared
• Targeted 'reactionaries' and 'anarchists' (anyone opposing the regime)

Results of the Red Terror:
• Destroyed all civilian opposition groups mercilessly
• Uprooted EPRP from all cities and towns
• Split within EPRP hastened its collapse
• Surviving members retreated to the countryside to form Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Army (EPRA)

Background:
• Somalia's irredentist ambition to annex the Ogaden
• Somali President Siad Barre saw the Derg's problems as opportunity to attack

Course of the War:
• Somalia launched full-scale invasion
• Ethiopian forces outnumbered in manpower and weapons, forced to retreat
• Within months, Somali forces captured large parts of the Ogaden, threatened Harar and Dire Dawa

Ethiopian Response:
• PMAC issued general mobilization
• Massive response from Ethiopian people, rallying behind the PMAC
• About 100,000 peasant militia trained at Tateq Training Camp
• Ethiopians launched counter-offensive, routed Somali invaders in weeks

External Support:
• Soviet Union, Cuba, and Democratic Republic of Yemen supported Ethiopia
• Ethiopia received Russian weapons and Cuban troops
• Somalia expelled Soviets and broke diplomatic relations

Outcome:
• Major realignment of power in the Horn of Africa
• Ethiopia broke off relations with the US completely
• Soviet Union became Ethiopia's primary ally

slide_title: The Derg and the Armed Struggle in Eritrea
basic_presentation:
After the Ogaden War: PMAC turned against Eritrean secessionists.

Initial Success:
• Massive human and material resources deployed
• Substantial gains in rural areas, secessionists forced to pull back
• Major towns captured, road from Addis Ababa to Asmara opened

EPLF Response:
• Sustained heavy losses but survived
• Regrouped in the Naqfa area
• Government failed to dislodge the EPLF from Naqfa

Turning Point:
• 1988: Afabet fell to the EPLF (major defeat for the Derg)
• 1990: Massawa captured by EPLF
• Decisive blow to the government army

slide_title: The Northern Insurgency and Downfall of the Derg
basic_presentation:
Soviet Policy Changes (Late 1980s):
• Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika
• Reduced military assistance to Ethiopia
• Collapse of the Soviet Union (1991)
• US became the sole undisputed global power

TPLF Advances:
• History traced back to 1975
• Mid-1980s: Consolidated, repulsed Derg offensives
• Captured several small towns in Tigray
• February 1989: Captured Enda Sellase

EPRDF Formation:
• TPLF abandoned initial objective of Tigray republic
• Merged with other groups to form Ethiopian Peoples' Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF)
• Founding members: TPLF, EPDM, OPDO, EDORM

Final Phase:
• March 1988: Nadew Command routed by EPLF
• May 1989: Aborted coup attempt; top generals arrested and executed
• 1990-1991: EPRDF advanced into Gondar, Gojjam, Wollo, Shewa
• May 21, 1991: Mengistu fled to Harare, Zimbabwe
• May 28, 1991: EPRDF forces entered Addis Ababa
• EPLF took complete control of Eritrea (de facto independence)

slide_title: The Road to Independence in Africa
basic_presentation:
National liberation movements took two courses: violent and non-violent.

West African Independence (Peaceful):
• No significant number of white settlers
• Long history of nationalist movements

British West Africa:
• Gold Coast (Ghana) - led by Kwame Nkrumah - independent March 1957
• Nigeria - led by Nnamdi Azikwe - independent October 1960
• Sierra Leone - independent April 1961
• Gambia - independent February 1964

French West Africa:
• 1958: de Gaulle offered choice between autonomy (within French Community) or independence
• Guinea voted 'No' - independent 1958 (first)
• Other colonies voted 'Yes' initially
• By November 1960, all French West African colonies achieved full independence

Africa Year (1960):
• Seventeen French colonies achieved independence
• Cameroon, Togo, Dahomey, Niger, Upper Volta, Ivory Coast, Chad
• Ubangi Shari, Middle Congo, Gabon, Senegal, French Sudan, Mauritania

Settler Colonies (Violent Independence):
• Significant number of white settlers made independence difficult

Algerian War of Independence (1954-1962):
• Algeria had been a French colony since 1830
• About one million white settlers (colons)
• Leaders: Ben Bella and the National Liberation Front (FLN)
• January 1961: Referendum, 75% voted for independence
• Evian Agreement (March 18, 1962) - ended the war
• July 1, 1962: Algeria became independent
• Ben Bella became first President

Post-independence African states faced political instability.

Military Coups:
• Most frequent means of changing government in 1960s-1980s
• Coup followed coup in Togo, Dahomey (Benin)
• Nigeria and Ghana experienced coups (1966)

Reasons for Military Involvement:
• Legacy of colonial rule
• Corruption in civilian regimes
• Military seen as disciplined and free from corruption

Examples of Tyrannical Rulers:
• General 'Emperor' Jean Bedel Bokassa (Central African Republic)
• Field Marshal Idi Amin (Uganda) - killed thousands, looted the economy
• Francisco Macias Nguema (Equatorial Guinea) - killed/thousands died

Nigeria:
• Civil war (1967-70) over Biafra secession
• General Gowon achieved post-war reconciliation
• 1975: General Murtala Muhammed overthrew Gowon, set timetable for civilian rule
• 1976: Muhammed assassinated, General Obasanjo took power, returned to civilian rule (1979)

1966: Kwame Nkrumah overthrown
• Blamed for prioritizing external affairs over domestic problems
• Forced into exile in Guinea

1972: Colonel Ignatius Acheampong staged coup
• 'Operation Feed Yourself' - aimed at reducing food imports
• Unable to halt overall economic decline

1979: Flight Lieutenant Jerry Rawlings seized power
• Three former military heads executed for corruption
• Returned to civilian rule within three months

December 1981: Rawlings seized power again
• Proclaimed a 'people's revolution'
• Removed old political elites from power

slide_title: Economy and Society in Independent Africa
basic_presentation:
Major Problem: Lack of economic diversity

Colonial Legacy:
• Africans encouraged to produce raw materials only
• Little effort to establish factories
• Specialization in single cash-crop products
• Unstable prices in world markets

Economic Crisis:
• International debt and drought (1980s-1990s)
• 22 countries could not feed their populations (1985)
• Agricultural production declined in early 1980s

Positive Examples:
• Botswana, Algeria, Gabon, Cote d'Ivoire recorded substantial achievements

Political Legacy:
• Colonial misrule had great impact on development
• Struggles for economic independence continued

Africa was a hotspot for Cold War rivalry between USA and USSR.

Soviet Involvement:
• Clear anti-imperialist ideology
• Gamal Abdel Nasser (Egypt) - first to seek Soviet support (Suez Crisis, 1956)
• Sekou Toure (Guinea) - turned to Soviets after French expulsion
• Soviet support for Mali, Ghana, Algeria
• By 1970s, Soviet Union became leading arms dealer in sub-Saharan Africa
• From $2 million (1974) to $3.4 billion (1979) in arms sales

US Involvement:
• Initially deferred to European allies
• Ethiopia (1953-1977): Major recipient of US aid
• After Derg came to power, US supported Somalia
• Egypt: Under Sadat, received US support after Yom Kippur War (1973)
• Libya: Bad relations with US (Gaddafi's hostility to Israel, support for terrorism)

slide_title: Settler Colonialism: Mozambique, Angola, and Zimbabwe
basic_presentation:
Portuguese Colonies:
• Angola and Mozambique had significant white settlers
• Liberation struggles started in early 1960s

Angola:
• Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA) - led by Agostino Neto
• 1975: Portuguese withdrawal, power struggle with UNITA
• MPLA government established, but continued civil war

Mozambique:
• Front for the Liberation of Mozambique (FRELIMO) - led by Eduardo Mondlane, then Samora Machel
• 1975: Mozambique gained independence

Zimbabwe (Southern Rhodesia):
• White minority government (1970: declared a republic)
• ZANU (Robert Mugabe) and ZAPU (Joshua Nkomo) fought liberation war
• 1979: Internal settlement, adopted name Zimbabwe
• April 18, 1980: Internationally recognized independence
• Mugabe became first Prime Minister

slide_title: The End of Apartheid in South Africa
basic_presentation:
Apartheid System (1948-early 1990s):
• Institutionalized racial segregation and discrimination
• Afrikaner National Party won 1948 election, strengthened segregation

Key Laws:
• Population Registration Act (1950): Classified people by race
• Group Areas Act (1950): Designated residential areas by race
• Bantu Education Act (1953): Prevented black South Africans from quality education

Resistance Movements:
• African National Congress (ANC) - founded 1912
• Leaders: Nelson Mandela, Oliver Tambo, Walter Sisulu
• March 21, 1960: Sharpeville Massacre (69 killed, 180 wounded)

Turning Points:
• ANC and PAC banned (1960)
• ANC established armed wing (Umkhonto we Sizwe)
• 1963: Mandela and others sentenced to life imprisonment

International Response:
• UN condemned apartheid, but sanctions blocked by UK and US (veto)
• South Africa withdrew from Commonwealth (1961)

End of Apartheid:
• 1970s: Black Consciousness movement
• 1980s: Mass protests, boycotts, strikes
• 1990: Nelson Mandela released
• 1994: First democratic elections - Mandela became President

slide_title: Pan-Africanism and the Organization of African Unity (OAU)
basic_presentation:
Pan-Africanism:
• Expression of desire for African unity and unity of all black peoples
• Originated in the Americas (Afro-Americans, Caribbean)
• Early leaders: W.E.B. Du Bois (Father of Pan-Africanism), Marcus Garvey (Back to Africa Movement)

Pan-African Conferences:
• First: London (1900) - organized by H. Sylvester Williams
• Five conferences before 1945
• Fifth: Manchester (1945) - landmark (African leaders participated)
   - Demanded African independence
   - Participants: Kwame Nkrumah, Jomo Kenyatta

Organization of African Unity (OAU):
• Founded May 1963 in Addis Ababa
• 32 African states signed the charter
• Primary aims:
   - Coordinate and intensify cooperation
   - Defend sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independence
   - Eradicate all forms of colonialism and white minority rule

slide_title: The OAU: Successes, Failures, and Transition to AU
basic_presentation:
Two Opposing Blocs:
• Casablanca Group: Immediate political union (Ghana, Algeria, Guinea, Morocco, Egypt, Mali, Libya)
• Monrovia Group: Gradual economic integration first (Ethiopia, Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Togo, Tunisia, Congo Kinshasa, Somalia)

Emperor Haile Selassie's Role:
• Bridged the gap between the two groups
• Invited leaders to Addis Ababa
• Succeeded in creating the OAU in 1963

OAU Achievements:
• Helped African countries achieve independence
• Supported anti-apartheid and liberation struggles
• African Development Bank established

OAU Failures:
• Criticized as 'Dictators' Club' or 'Dictator's Trade Union'
• No military wing to enforce decisions
• Policy of non-interference (could not stop civil wars)
• Could not condemn human rights violations by member states

African Union (AU):
• Sirte Declaration (September 1999) - called for new organization
• Inaugurated July 2002 in Durban, South Africa
• Stronger focus on economic and political integration
• Established Peace and Security Council, Pan-African Parliament, Human Rights institutions

Establishment:
• June 28, 1991: Derg regime overthrown
• EPRDF facilitated the establishment of Transitional Government of Ethiopia (TGE)
• National Conference in Addis Ababa (June 1991)
• 'Transitional Period Charter' adopted

Key Changes:
• New ethnic and language-based administrative structure
• 14 regions replaced previous 14 geographic provinces
• Former Ethiopian Armed Forces dismantled
• Ex-soldiers demobilized and became jobless

Drafting the Constitution:
• Constituent Assembly established
• Draft constitution presented for 'public discussion'
• Constitution of FDRE endorsed in August 1995

Key Features of the 1995 Constitution:
• Recognized human and democratic rights
• Recognized international regional declarations on human rights
• Recognized rights of nations, nationalities, and peoples for self-determination

Article 39 (Controversial):
• 'Every Ethiopian Nation, Nationality and people has an unconditional right to self-determination'
• 'Every Nation, Nationality and People has the right to a full measure of self-government'
• Critics argue this encourages secession and is dangerous for the country's survival

Federal Structure:
• 9 regions and 2 city states (Addis Ababa, Dire Dawa)
• Later: Sidama and Southwestern Ethiopian regional states added
• Based on language and ethnicity

Political Ideology:
• Revolutionary Democracy - ideology of the EPRDF-led government
• Economy based on agriculture

Elections Conducted: 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015

1995 Election:
• Some parties boycotted (All-Amhara Peoples' Organization, etc.)
• EPRDF won majority and formed government

2000 Election:
• Many parties participated (including those who boycotted previously)
• EPRDF again claimed landslide victory

2005 Election (Most Significant):
• Opposition parties united and better organized
• Coalition for Unity and Democracy (CUD) formed
• 90% voter turnout reported
• CUD won 180 seats (all 23 seats in Addis Ababa)
• NEBE declared EPRDF won 50%+1 vote
• Opposition rejected results
• Protests led to deaths and arrests
• CUD leaders sentenced to life imprisonment (later pardoned)

2010 and 2015 Elections:
• Less optimism
• EPRDF claimed majority of seats

Causes: Boundary dispute over Badme

Course of the War:
• May 6, 1998: Eritrean forces attacked Badme
• May 13, 1998: Ethiopian forces launched counter-offensive

International Mediation:
• USA and Rwanda proposed peace plan (evacuation of Eritrean troops)
• Eritrea rejected, called for demilitarization and direct talks

Operation Sunset (February 22, 1999):
• Ethiopia launched massive military offensive
• Recaptured most contested territories (Badme, Zalambessa)
• May 25, 1999: Ethiopia declared the war over

Casualties: Tens of thousands killed on both sides

Algiers Agreement (June 18, 2000):
• Comprehensive peace agreement signed
• 25km Temporary Security Zone (TSZ) established
• UNMEE deployed to patrol the zone

Boundary Commission Ruling (April 13, 2002):
• Awarded Badme to Eritrea
• Ethiopia requested further explanation, didn't implement decision
• 'No peace no war' situation for over a decade

Resolution:
• Relations improved after Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power

Economic Policy Shift:
• From command economy to market-oriented economy
• Capital limit for private investors lifted
• Government still participated in the economy

Land Issue:
• Land remained state property
• No private ownership of land

Agriculture:
• Agricultural Development-Led Industrialization (ADLI)
• Fertilizers and improved seeds increased yields
• Agricultural extension workers trained in large numbers
• Model peasants rewarded

Infrastructure Development:
• Road infrastructure and education: top budget sectors
• Universal Electrification Access Program (UEAP)
• Telecommunications infrastructure expanded

Great Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD):
• Foundation stone laid (2011) by Prime Minister Meles Zenawi
• Capacity: 6000 Mega Watts
• Financed by Ethiopian people (bonds)
• Source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over Nile water rights
• Ethiopia not a signatory to 1929 and 1959 Nile treaties

slide_title: Ethiopia's Role in Peacekeeping and Counter-Terrorism
basic_presentation:
UN Peacekeeping Missions:
• Long history dating back to the 1950s
• Korea, Congo, Rwanda, Burundi, Liberia, Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia
• Currently 8,297 troops, police, and military experts deployed

AU Peacekeeping:
• African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM)
• 4,395 uniformed personnel to the operation

Fighting Terrorism:
• Active participation in combating terrorism
• Worked to prevent Somalia from becoming a safe haven
• Collaborated with international community (especially US)
• Launched punitive military campaigns within Somalia
• Targeted Al-Shabaab terrorist group

Definition:
• Knowledge systems and practices developed outside the formal educational system
• Based on centuries of experimentation to cope with agro-ecological and socio-economic environments
• Also called traditional knowledge, local knowledge, folk knowledge

Unique Characteristics:
1. Local: Rooted in a particular place
2. Adaptive: Based on historical experiences, adapts to change
3. Cumulative: Developed from centuries of living in proximity to nature
4. Holistic: All aspects of life are interconnected
5. Humble: Lives in harmony with nature, not controlling it
6. Intergenerational: Passed from one generation to the next
7. Invaluable: Key to sustainable social and economic development
8. Irreplaceable: Cannot be replicated by western science
9. Moral: Has a right and wrong way to interact with nature
10. Relative: Knowledge varies by age and experience
11. Responsible: Responsibility for well-being of the environment
12. Spiritual: Rooted in social and spiritual relations
13. Valid: Does not require validation by western science

Ethiopia is rich in diverse indigenous knowledge systems in various areas.

Agriculture:
• Traditional farming techniques, terracing (Konso)

Architecture:
• Obelisk of Aksum, rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, castles of Gondar
• Wall of Harar

Medicine:
• Medicinal properties of many plants discovered

Cottage Industry:
• Iron smelting, tanning, weaving

Philosophy:
• Rich in oral and written philosophical literature (Ge'ez, Arabic)
• Proverbs, songs, folktales

Conflict Resolution:
• Traditional methods of conflict resolution

Examples:
• Gada system (Oromo) - indigenous democratic socio-political system
• Dagu system (Afar) - unique information exchange system ('Internet of the Afar')
• Luwa system (Sidama) - generational class system

slide_title: Heritages of Ethiopia: Definition and Types
basic_presentation:
Heritage Definition:
• Legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes inherited from past generations
• Both material and non-material culture

Values of Heritages:
• Promote interpretation of the past
• Commemorative value (collective memory and identity)
• Symbol of nationalism and national identity
• Instruments for nation-building

Types of Heritages:

Cultural Heritage:
• Tangible Cultural Heritage:
   - Movable: Manuscripts, paintings, sculptures, inscriptions
   - Immovable: Buildings, monuments, archaeological remains, palaces
• Intangible Cultural Heritage:
   - Performances, ceremonies, music, drama, literature
   - Religious, wedding, mourning ceremonies

Natural Heritage:
• National parks, gardens, mountain chains, natural areas

Literature (Ge'ez):
• Dominated by the Bible and Christian liturgy
• Hagiographies, literature about indigenous Ethiopian saints
• Works of history, ecclesiastical and civil law, philology, medicine
• Significant collections found outside Ethiopia (UK, France, Italy, Germany, US)

Al Nejashi Mosque:
• Oldest mosque in Ethiopia (Tigray)
• Established after the first followers of Prophet Mohammed sought refuge in Aksum (615 AD)
• King Ella Sham (Negash) granted them asylum

Palaces:
• Jimma Abba Jifar's Palace (18th century) - influenced by Indian architecture
• Kumsa Moreda's Palace (Wollega, 1870s)
• Sheikh Hojele's Residence (Addis Ababa)

Halala Kella (Dawuro):
• Defensive dry stone walls and ditches (16th-18th centuries)
• Built to protect against invaders
• Estimated length: 1,000 km total

Archaeological Sites:
• Lucy (Australopithecus afarensis) - named after Afar region
• Melka Kunture prehistoric site
• Tiya erected stones
• Awash and Omo valleys
• Hadar region (Afar)
• Fincha Habera site (Bale Mountains) - 30,000-year-old rock shelter (highest altitude human occupation)

Ethiopian Art:
• Christian art (paintings, crosses, icons, illuminated manuscripts)
• Lalibela Cross (12th century)
• Popular arts: textiles, basketry, jewelry
• Islamic illuminated manuscripts (Harar)
• Modern artists: Afework Tekle, Eskender Bogosian, Gebrekristos Desta, Agegnehu Engida

Music:
• Azmaris (wandering musicians)
• Yared - said to have invented musical notation
• Four major melodies: Bati, Tizeta, Ambassel, Anchihoye (gifts of Wollo)
• Modern music: 1960s-70s - Tilahun Gessesse, Ali Birra, Mahmoud Ahmed

Ashenda/Ashendiye/Solel:
• Celebrated in Tigray, Amhara, Agaw (August 16-26)
• Commemorates ascension of Virgin Mary
• Girls wear distinctive grass (Ashenda) around their waists
• Door-to-door celebrations, dancing, gifts

Timket (Ethiopian Epiphany):
• Commemorates baptism of Jesus (January 18-19)
• Ketera: Blocking water for blessing
• Tabots (replicas of Ark of the Covenant) processed

Meskel (Founding of the True Cross):
• Celebrated September 26
• Demera bonfire - decorated with Adey Abeba flowers
• Registered by UNESCO as World Heritage (September 2019)

Irreecha (Oromo Thanksgiving):
• Celebrated at beginning of spring (Birraa)
• At sacred lakes (Hora Harsadi, Bishoftu)
• Thanks Waaqa (God) for plentiful harvest

Fiche Chambalalla (Sidama New Year):
• Registered by UNESCO as World Heritage (September 2019)
• Communal events, traditional songs and dances
• Enhances equity, good governance, social cohesion

Gifaataa (Wolaita New Year Festival):
• Celebrates end of rainy season and beginning of warm season
• Peace-making and conflict resolution

Gada System (Oromo):
• Indigenous democratic socio-political system
• Age-grade classes and leadership rotation
• Registered by UNESCO as World Heritage

Luwa System (Sidama):
• Mentoring, training, and initiation system for youth
• Generational class or age-set system
• Administered by democratic rules and principles
• Leader called gadana, deputy called jalawa
• Five cycles: Fulasa, Darara, Mogisa, Wawasa, Hirbora
• Each cycle rotates approximately every eight years

Dagu System (Afar):
• Indigenous information exchange system
• Called the 'Internet of the Afar'
• Every Afar plays role of a journalist, elders as editors
• 'Wireless network' for sharing factual information

Cultural Heritage Sites:

• Tiya Stone Erections - UNESCO (1980)
   - 46 large, decorated megaliths
   - Cemetery site, dating between 10-15 centuries

• Harar Jugol, the Fortified Historic Town - UNESCO (2006)
   - 'Fourth city of Islam' - 82 mosques, 102 shrines
   - Five traditional gates (Asadin, Asum, Argob, Bedro, Sufat)
   - Hyena men tradition

• Rock-Hewn Churches of Lalibela - UNESCO (1978)
• Castles of Gondar - UNESCO (1979)
• Obelisks of Aksum
• Konso Cultural Landscape - UNESCO (2011)
   - 55 sq km arid property of stone-walled terraces

Intangible Cultural Heritage:
• Meskel Festival - UNESCO (2019)
• Fiche Chambalalla - UNESCO (2019)
• Gada System - UNESCO

Natural Heritage Site:
• Simen Mountains National Park - UNESCO (1978)
   - 220 sq km, famous for scenery, Gelada Baboon, Walia Ibex

Not Yet Registered: Bale Mountains National Park

slide_title: Ethical and Legal Issues in Information Systems
basic_presentation:
Ethics = principles of making right or wrong decisions
Technology creates new situations not covered by traditional laws
Four major ethical/legal issues:
  • Privacy – unauthorized access to personal data
  • Digital Ownership – controlling online creations
  • Information Gathering – consent for data collection
  • Information Security & Liability – protecting data and reporting breaches
In Ethiopia, report cyber breaches to INSA

Socialization Gaps – less real-world interaction
Cyberbullying – harmful content sent online
Social Media & Gaming Addiction – impairs life areas
Plagiarism – presenting others' work as your own
Cybercrime – fraud, identity theft, privacy violations
Automation & Job Displacement – routine jobs lost, new skills needed
Students should be mindful, responsible digital citizens

E-waste – discarded electronics with toxic materials
Hazardous substances: cadmium, lead, mercury
E-waste Management – systematic collection, recycling, safe disposal
Green/Clean Technology – eco-friendly solutions (solar, EVs)
Paperless systems – reduce deforestation
Responsibility: use and dispose of tech smartly

Mental health: sleeping disorders, stress, loss of attention
Musculoskeletal problems: back, neck, shoulders, wrists
Vision problems: eye strain, headaches
Obesity from prolonged sitting
Solution: take breaks, maintain good posture, use devices responsibly
Balance benefits of health IT with mindful usage

Intellectual Property = intangible rights over creative works
Four types relevant to IT:
  • Trade Secrets – confidential business info (e.g., Coca-Cola recipe)
  • Patents – exclusive rights for inventions (e.g., Google PageRank)
  • Copyrights – automatic protection for original works (e.g., software)
  • Trademarks – signs distinguishing goods/services (e.g., Microsoft logo)
Ethiopian Intellectual Property Office (EIPO) manages IP applications

Digital Identity = online collection of information about a person
Management involves:
  • Limiting data given out
  • Avoiding excessive storage
  • Checking and correcting personal data
Verification methods: documents, biometrics, database checks
Ethiopia: National ID project under Digital Ethiopia 2025 strategy

Digital collaboration = working together using digital tools
Three components:
  • People – heart of collaboration
  • Collaborative Tools – communication, file sharing, project management
  • Devices – smartphones, tablets, laptops
Tool examples: Teams, Zoom, Google Drive, Trello, Tableau, OneNote
Improves productivity, communication, and efficiency

Digital citizenship = responsible technology use
Good citizenship:
  • Make community better
  • Engage respectfully online
  • Make your voice heard
  • Validate online sources
Poor citizenship: cyberbullying, careless sharing, ignoring safety
Example: #It_is_my_dam campaign for GERD awareness

Big Data = massive, complex datasets hard to process traditionally
5 V's of Big Data:
  • Volume – enormous amount of data
  • Variety – structured, unstructured, semi-structured data
  • Velocity – speed data is created
  • Value – extracting useful insights
  • Veracity – reliability of data
Applications: healthcare, education, banking, agriculture, retail, transport
Challenges: growth, security, lack of skilled professionals

Delivery of computing services over the Internet
Benefits: accessibility, flexibility, auto-updates, cost-effective
Limitations: downtime, security/privacy, data ownership concerns
4 Types: Public, Private, Hybrid, Community
3 Service Models:
  • SaaS – ready-to-use software (e.g., Gmail)
  • PaaS – platform for development (e.g., Windows Azure)
  • IaaS – virtualized infrastructure (e.g., AWS)
Examples: Google Maps, Netflix, Spotify

Extension of cloud computing – processes data closer to source
Fog nodes near data sources have higher processing power
Benefits: low latency, location awareness, reduced bandwidth use
Processes data locally then sends summary to cloud
Essential for real-time applications (autonomous vehicles, smart traffic)
Bridges gap between IoT devices and the cloud

Network of physical objects with sensors to collect/exchange data
Advantages: efficiency, time-saving, improved decisions
Disadvantages: security risks, complexity, high cost
4 Components:
  • Sensors/Devices – collect data
  • Connectivity – transfer data
  • Data Processing – analyze data
  • User Interface – present information
Applications: Smart Home, Smart City, Supply Chain, Healthcare

RDBMS = software to create, maintain, and access relational databases
Relational database = data stored in 2D tables
Fields/Columns/Attributes – represent properties
Records/Rows/Tuples – represent single entries
Data Types: Text, Integer, Date/Time, Currency
Primary Key – uniquely identifies each record
Foreign Key – links tables (primary key in another table)
Examples: Access, Oracle, MySQL, SQLite

SQL = Structured Query Language for databases
Launch Access → Create blank database
Create Query → Switch to SQL View
Write SQL commands in SQL View
Run query using 'Run' button (Design tab)
Common commands: CREATE, SELECT, UPDATE, INSERT
Double-click saved query to run later

DDL: Create and restructure database objects
Commands:
  • CREATE TABLE – define new table with columns and data types
  • ALTER TABLE – modify existing table (add, drop, change columns)
  • DROP TABLE – delete table completely
Common data types: CHAR, TEXT, INTEGER, DATETIME, CURRENCY
REFERENCES keyword creates foreign key relationships
Careful: DROP TABLE is permanent

DML: Manage data in tables
Commands:
  • INSERT – add new records
  • UPDATE – modify existing records
  • DELETE – remove records
Use WHERE clause in UPDATE and DELETE to target specific rows
Without WHERE: all rows are affected!
For DELETE, foreign key constraints may prevent deletion

SELECT = retrieve data from database
Basic syntax: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... ORDER BY ...
SELECT * FROM table – all records
SELECT column1, column2 – limited columns
WHERE – filter records with conditions
ORDER BY – sort results (ASC/DESC)
Join tables: SELECT ... FROM table1, table2 WHERE table1.key = table2.key

XML = store and structure data, not present it
Components of XML document:
  • XML Declaration – version, encoding
  • Document Type Declaration (DTD) – document structure
  • Root Element – single parent element
  • Start/End Tags – define elements
  • Data – content between tags
  • Attributes – name-value pairs
  • Comments – ignored by parser
Syntax rules: one root, case-sensitive, proper nesting, quoted attributes

HTML: Presentation/display of data
XML: Storage/transport of data
Key differences:
  • HTML = predefined tags; XML = custom tags
  • HTML = format-driven; XML = content-driven
  • HTML = case-insensitive; XML = case-sensitive
  • HTML = tolerant of errors; XML = strict, no errors
  • HTML = .html; XML = .xml
They are complementary, not competing

Advantages:
  • Transportable across systems
  • Separates data from HTML
  • Simplifies platform exchange
Disadvantages:
  • Needs processing application
  • Confusing syntax
  • No intrinsic data types
  • Redundant/syntactically heavy

Website = organized files with root directory
Root has subfolders: pages, images, CSS, scripts
index.html = default homepage
Publishing = upload files to web host's remote server
Domain name = unique website address (e.g., moe.gov.et)
Domain extensions: .com, .edu, .gov, .org, .mil, .net
Security: HTTPS + SSL certificate (encrypts data)
Secure sites show locked padlock in browser

PC Installation:
  • Insert installation disc or download from source
  • Run installation program
  • Follow on-screen instructions
  • Agree to license, enter serial number
  • Restart if prompted
Mobile Installation:
  • Use trusted app stores only (Google Play, Apple App Store)
